title: Prompting Patterns for Agents
summary: Prompting an agent is not the same as chatting with a model. Because an agent runs in a loop, calls tools, and must produce parseable output, its prompt has to nail the role and goal, show format by example, decompose the task, name the tools explicitly, and add guardrails against rambling — trading conversational flair for determinism and control.

subtopics.title: State the role and the goal up front
subtopics.explanation: The system prompt should pin down who the agent is, what it is trying to achieve, and what 'done' looks like, so it does not drift or invent scope. A vague persona produces vague, meandering behavior; a sharp role and a single measurable goal keep every loop pointed the same direction. This framing is the foundation that all the other prompting patterns build on.
subtopics.example:
SYSTEM = (
    "You are a support triage agent. "
    "Goal: classify the ticket into exactly one category "
    "and decide whether it needs a human.\n"
    "You are DONE when you output the final JSON verdict. "
    "Do not answer the customer directly."
)
messages = [{"role": "system", "content": SYSTEM}]

subtopics.title: Show, don't tell: few-shot examples
subtopics.explanation: Instead of describing the desired behavior in prose, include a couple of input/output examples so the model can pattern-match the exact shape you want. Few-shot examples are especially powerful for edge cases and formatting because they demonstrate rather than describe. For an agent this steers it toward the same structured output every time, which is the whole game.
subtopics.example:
FEWSHOT = [
    {"role": "user", "content": "My invoice is wrong."},
    {"role": "assistant", "content": '{"category": "billing", "needs_human": true}'},
    {"role": "user", "content": "How do I reset my password?"},
    {"role": "assistant", "content": '{"category": "account", "needs_human": false}'},
]
messages = [{"role": "system", "content": SYSTEM}] + FEWSHOT
# the model now imitates the demonstrated JSON shape

subtopics.title: Specify the output format precisely
subtopics.explanation: Tell the model exactly what structure to return — the field names, types, and that nothing else should surround it — because downstream code has to parse it. Ambiguous format instructions are the number-one cause of parse failures in agents. Nailing the format is what lets the loop hand results to your code without a fragile cleanup step.
subtopics.example:
FORMAT = (
    "Respond with ONLY a JSON object, no prose, no code fences:\n"
    "{\"category\": <string>, \"needs_human\": <boolean>, \"reason\": <string>}"
)
messages.append({"role": "system", "content": FORMAT})
# pair this with temperature=0 so the structure stays stable

subtopics.title: Decompose the task into explicit steps
subtopics.explanation: Break a complex goal into an ordered checklist inside the prompt so the model tackles one sub-goal at a time instead of leaping to a conclusion. Decomposition reduces reasoning errors and makes each loop's action predictable and auditable. For an agent this turns a fuzzy objective into a sequence of tool calls you can follow and debug.
subtopics.example:
PLAN = (
    "Work through these steps in order:\n"
    "1. Read the ticket text.\n"
    "2. Pick the single best category.\n"
    "3. If the issue risks money or data loss, set needs_human=true.\n"
    "4. Emit the final JSON verdict and stop."
)
messages.append({"role": "system", "content": PLAN})

subtopics.title: Be explicit about tools and add guardrails
subtopics.explanation: Spell out which tools exist, when to use each, and what to do on failure — and add constraints that stop the model from rambling, apologizing, or inventing tools. Agent prompting differs from chatbot prompting precisely here: you often force a tool call, forbid free-form chatter, and cap the reasoning so the loop stays cheap and deterministic. These guardrails are what make an agent production-safe rather than merely conversational.
subtopics.example:
GUARDRAILS = (
    "Tools: lookup_order(order_id), escalate(reason). "
    "Use lookup_order before deciding; never invent an order_id. "
    "If a tool errors, report the error in 'reason' and set needs_human=true. "
    "Do NOT write apologies, explanations, or extra prose. "
    "Output at most one JSON object."
)
messages.append({"role": "system", "content": GUARDRAILS})
# tool-forcing + no-rambling = predictable loops

foundations.overview: A chatbot prompt optimizes for a helpful, natural reply to a human; an agent prompt optimizes for a machine-parseable action inside a loop. The core patterns are: frame a precise role and a single measurable goal, demonstrate the desired output with few-shot examples, specify the exact output format, decompose the task into ordered steps, and be explicit about the available tools while adding guardrails against rambling or hallucinated tools. Together these push the agent toward deterministic, auditable behavior — usually paired with a low temperature — so your code can reliably consume what it produces.
foundations.formalDefinition: Agent prompting is the practice of engineering the system and few-shot context to constrain an LLM's outputs to structured, tool-oriented actions: role/goal framing, demonstration (few-shot), format specification, decomposition, and explicit tool/guardrail instructions, tuned for reliability rather than conversational quality.
foundations.whyItMatters: In an agent loop, one badly formatted or rambling response cascades: it fails to parse, triggers a retry, wastes tokens, and can send the loop off course. Good prompting patterns are the cheapest, highest-leverage way to raise an agent's reliability before you reach for retries, validators, or fine-tuning.
foundations.mentalModel: Think of chatbot prompting as briefing a helpful colleague and agent prompting as writing a strict work order for a contractor: exact deliverable, exact format, the tools they may use, the steps to follow, and a firm 'no extra chatter'. The tighter the work order, the more predictable the result.
foundations.realWorldUsage: Writing system prompts for tool-calling agents, adding few-shot examples to stabilize JSON output, forcing a specific tool on the first turn of a workflow, and adding 'no prose / output only the object' guardrails to keep downstream parsers happy.
commonUseCases: System prompts that fix role, goal, and 'done' criteria
Few-shot examples to lock in output format and edge cases
Tool-forcing and anti-rambling guardrails for reliability

commonMisconceptions.myth: Prompting an agent is just prompting a chatbot with more words.
commonMisconceptions.reality: Agents need parseable, tool-oriented output and predictable loops. You optimize for determinism and format compliance, not for a pleasant conversational tone.

commonMisconceptions.myth: Politeness like 'please answer only in JSON' is enough to guarantee format.
commonMisconceptions.reality: Prose instructions help but are not a guarantee. Pair them with few-shot examples, low temperature, and a validator + retry — prompting reduces failures, it does not eliminate them.

commonMisconceptions.myth: Longer, more detailed prompts always give better agents.
commonMisconceptions.reality: Bloated prompts burn context budget and can dilute attention. Tight role, crisp format, a couple of examples, and clear guardrails usually beat a wall of instructions.

interactiveExamples.title: Vague prompt vs. structured agent prompt
interactiveExamples.explanation: The same task with a loose chatbot-style instruction versus a role/goal/format-constrained agent prompt. Watch how the second version forces a parseable object instead of chatty prose.

code.code:
# chatbot-style: friendly but unparseable
vague = [
    {"role": "user", "content": "Can you help me figure out what this support ticket is about?"}
]

# agent-style: role + goal + explicit format
structured = [
    {"role": "system", "content": (
        "You are a ticket-triage agent. Goal: classify the ticket. "
        "Respond with ONLY this JSON: "
        '{\"category\": <string>, \"needs_human\": <boolean>}'
    )},
    {"role": "user", "content": "My invoice is wrong and I was double charged."},
]

print("vague expects:", "free-form paragraph (hard to parse)")
print("structured expects:", '{"category": "billing", "needs_human": true}')
code.caption: The structured prompt turns an open question into a fixed, machine-readable action.
code.expectedOutput:
vague expects: free-form paragraph (hard to parse)
structured expects: {"category": "billing", "needs_human": true}

interactiveExamples.title: Composing a full agent system prompt
interactiveExamples.explanation: A reusable builder that layers the patterns — role/goal, format, decomposition, tools, and guardrails — into one system message plus few-shot examples, the way you would ship it.

code.code:
def build_agent_prompt(role, goal, tools, output_schema):
    return (
        f"You are {role}.\n"
        f"Goal: {goal}\n"
        "Steps: (1) inspect input (2) use a tool if needed (3) emit the verdict and stop.\n"
        f"Tools available: {', '.join(tools)}. Never invent a tool.\n"
        f"Respond with ONLY this JSON, no prose or code fences: {output_schema}\n"
        "If a tool errors, set needs_human=true and explain in 'reason'."
    )

system = build_agent_prompt(
    role="a support triage agent",
    goal="classify the ticket and decide if a human is needed",
    tools=["lookup_order", "escalate"],
    output_schema='{"category": <string>, "needs_human": <bool>, "reason": <string>}',
)

fewshot = [
    {"role": "user", "content": "Where is my order #123?"},
    {"role": "assistant", "content": '{"category": "shipping", "needs_human": false, "reason": "standard status lookup"}'},
]
messages = [{"role": "system", "content": system}] + fewshot
print(len(messages), "messages ready; call with temperature=0")
code.caption: Layering the patterns into one composable builder keeps agent prompts consistent across a codebase.

theory.question: How does prompting an agent differ from prompting a chatbot?
theory.directAnswer: Chatbot prompting optimizes for a helpful, natural reply to a human; agent prompting optimizes for structured, tool-oriented actions inside a loop, so it emphasizes precise output format, explicit tool guidance, decomposition, guardrails against rambling, and low temperature for determinism.

detailedExplanation.whatItIs: Agent prompting is engineering the system and few-shot context so an LLM reliably emits machine-parseable actions rather than conversational text.
detailedExplanation.whyItExists: An agent's output is consumed by code, not a person. If it rambles, adds code fences, or invents a tool, the parse fails, a retry fires, tokens are wasted, and the loop can go off course.
detailedExplanation.howItWorks: You fix a role and measurable goal, demonstrate the exact output with few-shot examples, specify the format explicitly and forbid extra prose, decompose the task into ordered steps, name the available tools with usage and failure rules, and typically run at temperature 0 to keep the structure stable.

theory.whyImportant: Prompting is the cheapest, highest-leverage reliability lever in an agent; getting these patterns right prevents most parse failures before you reach for validators, retries, or fine-tuning.
theory.realWorldExample: A triage agent's system prompt states the role and goal, shows two few-shot classifications, demands 'ONLY this JSON object, no prose', lists lookup_order and escalate, and forbids inventing tools — cutting malformed outputs dramatically.

followUps.question: Why pair format instructions with few-shot examples?
followUps.answer: Prose describes the format; examples demonstrate it. Demonstration is stronger for edge cases and formatting, and together they raise compliance more than either alone.

followUps.question: How does temperature relate to prompting for agents?
followUps.answer: Even a perfect prompt can drift under high temperature. Running near 0 keeps the well-formed, most-likely tokens dominant, so the format instructions actually hold.

theory.question: What are the main guardrails you add to an agent prompt and why?
theory.directAnswer: Common guardrails are: forbid inventing tools, forbid extra prose or code fences, define what to do on tool failure, cap the reasoning or steps, and force a specific output shape. They keep the loop deterministic, parseable, cheap, and safe.

detailedExplanation.whatItIs: Guardrails are explicit constraints in the prompt that bound the model's behavior so it cannot ramble, hallucinate capabilities, or produce output the parser can't consume.
detailedExplanation.whyItExists: A free-running agent tends to apologize, over-explain, wrap JSON in fences, or reference tools that don't exist — each of which breaks downstream code or wastes budget in the loop.
detailedExplanation.howItWorks: You enumerate the allowed tools and say 'never invent a tool', require 'output only the object, no prose', specify error handling ('if a tool errors, set needs_human=true'), and constrain length or steps so each loop is predictable and auditable.

theory.whyImportant: Guardrails are what turn a conversational model into a production-safe agent; without them reliability and cost both degrade as the loop runs.
theory.realWorldExample: Adding 'Do NOT write apologies or explanations; output at most one JSON object' to a support agent eliminated the wrapping text that had been breaking the JSON parser on roughly a fifth of turns.

followUps.question: What is tool-forcing?
followUps.answer: Instructing (or configuring the API) so the model must call a specific tool on a given turn, removing the choice to answer in free text — useful for the first, mandatory step of a workflow.

followUps.question: Can guardrails hurt?
followUps.answer: Yes — overly rigid prompts can cause the model to fail rather than adapt, and long guardrail text eats context budget, so you keep them tight and test them.

scenario.question: Your agent's outputs parse fine in testing but fail ~15% of the time in production with messages like 'Sure! Here is the JSON: ```json ...```'. How do you fix it with prompting patterns?
scenario.directAnswer: Tighten the prompt: demand ONLY the JSON object with no prose or code fences, add two few-shot examples showing the bare object, drop temperature to 0, and back it with a validator that strips/retries on any surrounding text — treating prompting as reduction, not a guarantee.

detailedExplanation.whatItIs: A format-compliance failure where the model wraps valid JSON in conversational text and fences that the parser rejects.
detailedExplanation.whyItExists: The prompt likely suggested rather than demanded the format, and higher production temperature plus varied inputs let the chatty tokens surface more often than in testing.
detailedExplanation.howItWorks: Replace soft language with 'Respond with ONLY a JSON object; no prose, no markdown fences.' Add few-shot pairs whose assistant turns are the bare object. Set temperature=0 so the well-formed tokens dominate. Then add a defensive parser that extracts the object and, on failure, re-prompts once with 'Return only the JSON object.'

scenario.whyImportant: It shows the layered reliability mindset: prompting reduces failures, examples and low temperature reinforce it, and a validator+retry catches the residual — the standard production pattern.
scenario.realWorldExample: After demanding the bare object, adding examples, and setting temperature 0, the wrapping-text failures dropped from ~15% to under 1%, and the retry caught the rest.

followUps.question: Why not just regex the JSON out of the prose?
followUps.answer: You can as a fallback, but it's fragile with nested braces or multiple objects. Fixing the prompt removes the prose at the source; the extractor is only a safety net.

followUps.question: Why did testing miss it?
followUps.answer: Tests likely used a few benign inputs at low temperature. Production has more varied prompts and often higher temperature, surfacing the chatty behavior the prompt never forbade.

coding.question: Write a function that composes an agent system prompt from a role, goal, tool list, and output schema, enforcing the core prompting patterns (format-only output, no invented tools, error handling).
coding.thoughtProcess: The patterns are stable, so a small builder that interpolates the variable parts keeps prompts consistent. I include role/goal framing, a decomposition line, explicit tools with a 'never invent' guardrail, a strict format instruction forbidding prose/fences, and a tool-failure rule. Returning a plain string keeps it provider-agnostic.

solution.code:
def build_agent_prompt(role: str, goal: str, tools: list[str], output_schema: str) -> str:
    tool_line = ", ".join(tools) if tools else "none"
    return (
        f"You are {role}.\n"
        f"Goal: {goal}\n"
        "Steps: (1) inspect the input (2) call a tool only if needed "
        "(3) emit the final verdict and stop.\n"
        f"Tools available: {tool_line}. Never invent or assume a tool.\n"
        f"Respond with ONLY this JSON object, no prose and no code fences: {output_schema}\n"
        "If a tool errors, set needs_human=true and explain in 'reason'."
    )

if __name__ == "__main__":
    prompt = build_agent_prompt(
        role="a support triage agent",
        goal="classify the ticket and decide if a human is needed",
        tools=["lookup_order", "escalate"],
        output_schema='{"category": <string>, "needs_human": <bool>, "reason": <string>}',
    )
    print("ONLY this JSON" in prompt and "Never invent" in prompt)

lineByLine: tool_line joins the tool names, defaulting to 'none' so an empty list still reads cleanly.
The role and goal lines frame identity and the single measurable objective.
The Steps line decomposes the task so the model acts in order rather than leaping to a conclusion.
The Tools line names allowed tools and adds the 'never invent' guardrail against tool hallucination.
The format line demands ONLY the object with no prose or fences — the key anti-rambling rule.
The final line defines tool-failure behavior so errors surface as data instead of crashing the loop.
The __main__ block asserts the critical guardrail phrases are present.
coding.timeComplexity: O(t) where t is the number of tools (for the join).
coding.spaceComplexity: O(n) in the length of the produced prompt string.

followUps.question: How would you add few-shot examples?
followUps.answer: Return the system string plus a list of user/assistant message pairs whose assistant turns are bare objects, then prepend the system message to that list before calling the model.

followUps.question: How do you keep the prompt from bloating context?
followUps.answer: Keep guardrails terse, reuse one schema string, and cap few-shot examples to two or three — enough to demonstrate the shape without eating the token budget.

keyTakeaways: Agent prompts optimize for parseable, tool-oriented actions in a loop — not for a natural chatbot reply.
Frame a precise role and a single measurable goal, and define exactly what 'done' means.
Show the desired output with few-shot examples and specify the format explicitly (only the object, no prose or fences).
Decompose complex tasks into ordered steps and be explicit about which tools exist and when to use them.
Add guardrails (no invented tools, no rambling, defined error handling) and run at low temperature; prompting reduces failures, so still back it with a validator and retry.
